source.title: Data Engineering for Scaling Language Models to 128K Context
source.authors: Yao Fu; Rameswar Panda; Xinyao Niu; Xiang Yue; Hanna Hajishirzi; Yoon Kim; Hao Peng

record.tranche_reason: The study reports that similar validation losses can accompany substantially different retrieval performance, refining the claim that pretraining loss predicts downstream performance. It does not test the original parameter/token/compute power-law fits.
record.gate_note: The study tests continual-pretraining token quantity and data-mixture choices, measuring long-context retrieval and BookQA. It does not fit scaling exponents or vary parameter count and compute at fixed budget. The paper's cited scaling-law results are not this study's results. Short-context MMLU is not a test of the listed downstream-predictability version.
record.test_reason: Only V6 is touched. Figure 3 pairs validation loss with Needle-in-a-Haystack retrieval across a 100M–10B continual-pretraining token sweep. Figure 4 shows two data mixtures with nearly equal validation loss but very different retrieval, so loss alone does not predict this downstream ability. There is no parameter or compute sweep and no fitted law. The setting is context-extension continual pretraining of LLaMA-2 7B, not from-scratch pretraining scaling.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that precise retrieval over long context is mostly acquired during standard pretraining. They find it can be unlocked to 128K with continual pretraining on 1–5B tokens of per-source length-upsampled data that keeps the domain balance; book-only or naive upsampling is suboptimal. They also caution that validation loss alone can conceal large differences in retrieval ability.
record.recipe_differences: The study varies continual-pretraining token quantity and data mixture to extend context length; it does not use the original scaling-law fitting or compute-optimal allocation method.
record.method_sensitivity: Retrieval and domain losses depend on training-token quantity and data composition; the authors report saturation and reduced length generalization at 10B tokens, and differing retrieval for mixtures with very close validation loss.
record.problems: The experiments concern a limited set of LLaMA-2 models and long-context tasks, not a broad model-size or compute sweep. Several retrieval accuracies are presented in figures without uncertainty estimates. No power-law exponents or compute-optimal allocations are fitted.
record.rows_left_out: Table 3's short-context MMLU results were left out because they do not measure the downstream-predictability claim as framed. Table 5's domain-specific validation-loss differences were left out because they do not themselves measure downstream task performance.

untested.parts: All: no extrapolation from small to large runs.
All: architecture is fixed apart from the RoPE base.
No power-law form is fitted for continual pretraining or any other regime.
Scaling with model size; any fitted or quantitative predictive relation; downstream tasks other than long-context retrieval; from-scratch pretraining.

missing.what: Per-length validation losses at each token quantity (e.g. 128K loss 1.61, 1.44, 1.34, 1.38, 1.36, 1.35 from 100M to 10B). These are needed to judge whether retrieval tracks loss.
Per-length validation losses for the two mixtures, e.g. 1.42 vs 1.41 at 32K and 1.37 vs 1.36 at 128K.

record.verdict_notes: This is a context-extension data-engineering paper, not a scaling-law study. Its link to V6 is narrow: it concerns continual-pretraining tokens and data mixture at fixed model size. Table 3 (MMLU) and Table 5 (domain losses) were correctly left out. The 13B results come from a single run and add no scaling evidence. No uncertainty estimates are reported anywhere.

versions.untested_parts: Power-law loss against parameter count, tokens, or compute over several orders of magnitude.
Whether fits on small runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its trend with compute.
Effects of depth, width, and architecture at fixed parameter count.
Power-law forms in other modalities or training regimes.
The study examines long-context retrieval and BookQA in a limited set of models and training conditions; it does not establish general predictability across downstream tasks or model scales.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocations on fitting choices and setup.

rows.subject: LLaMA-2 7B

rows.note: The paper describes retrieval performance as gradually increasing as the token quantity rises from 100M.
rows.check: Baseline is missing. This is the lowest point of the token sweep, and its 128K-context loss is 1.61 (Fig. 3). The authors say loss has not yet converged at 100M–300M tokens.

rows.subject: LLaMA-2 7B

rows.note: The authors report generalization to unseen lengths from 80K to 128K after 5B tokens.

rows.subject: LLaMA-2 7B
rows.operation_detail: Continual pretraining with varying token quantities; Needle-in-a-Haystack evaluation
rows.note: Accuracy falls from the 5B result; the authors say retrieval saturates around 5B and length generalization decreases at 10B as the model appears to overfit its 80K training range.
rows.check: Retrieval falls from 88.0 to 84.0 while Fig. 3 loss keeps falling (1K 1.80→1.79; 128K 1.36→1.35). This is a small reversal, with no uncertainty reported. The authors attribute it to saturation or overfitting to the 80K training range.

rows.subject: LLaMA-2 7B
rows.operation_detail: Continual pretraining on the original data mixture without length upsampling; Needle-in-a-Haystack evaluation
rows.baseline: Per-source length-upsampled mixture; validation loss described as very close
rows.note: The text says the original mixture, despite close validation loss, performs badly on precise retrieval relative to per-source length upsampling.
rows.check: Values can be read from Fig. 4: per-length losses are 1.80/1.56/1.42/1.33/1.37 vs 1.80/1.56/1.41/1.32/1.36. The figure text does not clearly assign which loss row belongs to which mixture. The state means loss fails to predict retrieval: equal loss, different retrieval.

rows.subject: LLaMA-2 7B
rows.operation_detail: Continual pretraining on per-source length-upsampled data; Needle-in-a-Haystack evaluation
rows.baseline: Original data mixture; validation loss described as very close
rows.note: The authors state that per-source length upsampling significantly improves precise retrieval despite validation loss being very close to the original-mixture model.
rows.check: This is the comparator in the R7 pair. On its own it shows the study's recommended mixture doing well, not whether retrieval tracks loss. Its evidence on V6 is carried by the R7 comparison.

relationships.condition: LLaMA-2 7B, continual pretraining on per-source-upsampled data, 100M to 5B tokens
relationships.reason: Retrieval rises monotonically (37.8, 59.0, 81.1, 85.3, 88.0) as validation loss falls. The authors say loss correlates with retrieval, though no predictive law is fitted (R1–R5).
relationships.display_finding: Retrieval rose from 37.8 through 59.0, 81.1, and 85.3 to 88.0 as validation loss decreased, without a fitted predictive law.

relationships.reason: Loss keeps decreasing slightly but retrieval drops from 88.0 to 84.0, which the authors attribute to overfitting to the 80K length (R5–R6).
relationships.display_finding: Retrieval fell from 88.0 to 84.0 as loss continued decreasing slightly, which the authors attributed to overfitting to the 80K context length.

relationships.condition: LLaMA-2 7B, 5B tokens at 80K: original vs per-source length-upsampled mixture
relationships.reason: Per-length validation losses differ by at most about 0.01, yet the original mixture 'performs badly on precise retrieval'. Loss therefore fails to predict downstream retrieval across data mixtures (R7–R8).
relationships.display_finding: Validation losses by sequence length differed by at most about 0.01, yet the original data mixture performed poorly on precise retrieval compared with the length-upsampled mixture.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
